lead: Some sensors read position or rotation without touching the part. The Hall sensor uses the Lorentz force on charge carriers in a thin semiconductor plate to make a small voltage proportional to magnetic field. A variable-reluctance sensor makes an AC pulse from a moving toothed wheel. An optical sensor breaks a light beam with a vane. These three give the ECU crank position, wheel speed and pedal position without wear, and each has a different output and a different tolerance to dirt.
prereq: You need: 3.3 crank position and the magnetic field and induction basics from physics.

blocks.text: A thin semiconductor plate carries current I. A magnetic field B at right angles pushes the moving carriers sideways with force q v × B. Charge collects on one edge until the electric field balances this force. The steady voltage across the plate is the Hall voltage. It is small, often millivolts, so an amplifier and a Schmitt trigger follow it.
V_H = K_H I B,  K_H = 1/(n q t)    and    V_H = R_H I B / t,  R_H = 1/(n q)
blocks.where: V_H is the Hall voltage in V; I is the current in A; B is the flux density in T; n is the carrier density in m⁻³; q is the carrier charge in C; t is the plate thickness in m; K_H is the Hall sensitivity (current-related sensitivity) in V/(A·T) or m²/C; R_H is the Hall coefficient in m³/C.

blocks.text: A Hall switch compares V_H with two thresholds. The output changes at the operate point and returns at the release point, so a small field wobble does not chatter. A Hall latch keeps its last state until the field reverses. Hall sensors are used for cam and crank position, wheel speed, pedal position and gear selection. Most are digital switches; linear Hall versions give an analog voltage that is used for pedal and throttle position. They need a supply; many work down to zero speed. Magnetoresistive sensors use a thin film whose resistance changes with field angle, giving a compact angle signal for some pedal and motor-position applications.

A variable-reluctance (VR) sensor has a coil wound on a magnet, facing a toothed iron wheel. As a tooth moves near the coil, the air gap and the magnetic reluctance fall; flux rises. As the tooth leaves, flux falls. The changing flux induces a voltage in the coil by Faraday's law. The sensor is passive: it needs no supply. It is also called a magnetic reluctance or inductive sensor.
e = -N dΦ/dt    and    f = z n / 60
blocks.where: e is the induced voltage in V; N is the number of turns; Φ is the magnetic flux in Wb; t is time in s; f is the pulse frequency in Hz; z is the number of teeth; n is the shaft speed in rev/min.

blocks.text: The output is an AC voltage. Its amplitude and frequency both rise with speed. At low speed the amplitude may be too small for the ECU, and at zero speed there is no output. Signal conditioning uses a threshold and often a zero-crossing detector to make a clean pulse. A VR sensor is robust and simple, and is common on older crank and ABS wheel-speed sensing. The air gap must be small and uniform; run-out or metal debris changes the pulse.

An optical sensor uses an LED and a phototransistor. In the slotted type, a vane on the moving part passes through the gap and blocks the light; the phototransistor switches. In the reflective type, light returns from a mark. The output is digital and works down to zero speed. Dirt, oil, water and strong ambient light can block or false-trigger the beam, so the gap is kept small and shielded. Some texts call these optoelectronic sensors.

Optical crankshaft position sensing uses a disc with slots fixed to the crank. The ECU counts slot edges for speed and uses one wider index slot for absolute position. A slotted coupler gives one pulse per slot; the index pulse marks top dead centre for cylinder 1. This is non-contact and has no wear, but it is less tolerant of oil mist than a Hall or VR sensor.
All three are non-contact, so there is no rubbing wear.
In the last column, High means the sensor works well despite dirt.

examples.question: A Hall plate carries I = 10 mA in a flux density B = 0.1 T. The plate thickness is t = 0.5 mm and carrier density is n = 1×10²² m⁻³. Take q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. Find V_H in volts and in millivolts.
examples.answer: The Hall voltage is 0.00125 V, or 1.25 mV; an amplifier raises this to a logic level.
examples.check:
I=10e-3
B=0.1
t=0.5e-3
n=1e22
q=1.6e-19
V=I*B/(n*q*t)
print(round(V,8))
print(round(V*1000,4))

traps: A VR sensor is not a Hall sensor: its output is an AC voltage that depends on speed, so it needs a threshold and often a zero-crossing detector. A Hall sensor needs a supply and gives a digital signal.
Hall voltage is proportional to B, but a Hall switch has hysteresis: the operate and release fields differ.
Convert mA to A and mm to m before using V_H = I B/(n q t); a factor of 1000 is the common slip.
Optical sensors fail with dirt, oil and sunlight; a missing pulse may be a blocked beam, not a bad ECU.
A passive VR sensor cannot report zero speed; no rotation means no flux change and no output.

quiz.q: What physical quantity does a Hall sensor convert to voltage?
quiz.a: Magnetic flux density B, with a fixed current, is converted to Hall voltage V_H.

quiz.q: Why is a Schmitt trigger placed after the Hall amplifier?
quiz.a: It converts a noisy analog voltage into a clean digital edge and adds hysteresis so small noise near the threshold does not cause extra pulses.

quiz.q: A VR sensor faces a wheel with 36 teeth turning at 1200 rev/min. Find the pulse frequency.
Compare Hall and VR sensors for crank position at cranking speed near zero.
quiz.a: VR output falls with speed and is absent at zero, so it cannot give position before motion; Hall needs a supply but gives a digital state at zero speed. VR is simple and passive; Hall needs a magnet and electronics.

quiz.q: Name the two main parts of a slotted optical sensor.
quiz.a: An LED light source and a phototransistor receiver.

quiz.q: Why can an optical crank sensor miss pulses in an oily engine bay?
quiz.a: Oil or dirt on the disc or lens blocks or scatters the beam, so the phototransistor does not switch at every slot.

quiz.q: For an ABS wheel-speed sensor on a dirty truck, choose between VR, Hall and optical. Give one reason.
quiz.a: A Hall sensor is a good choice: it gives a digital signal down to low speed and is less sensitive to dirt than optical. VR is robust and passive but weak at low speed; optical is worst with dirt.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production Hall ICs include the plate, amplifier, Schmitt trigger and sometimes a DSP in one package, with stray-field compensation. Magnetoresistive and tunnel-magnetoresistive sensors give higher sensitivity for fine angle measurement. Optical encoders are common in laboratory and motor test work, while automotive crank sensing mostly uses Hall or VR for cost and dirt tolerance. Search terms: Hall switch hysteresis, variable-reluctance sensor threshold, optical encoder quadrature.
